title: Shaka and the Buffalo Horns
text:
In the early 19th century the Zulu were a small chiefdom in what is now KwaZulu-Natal. Shaka kaSenzangakhona, who took power around 1816, had served in the army of Dingiswayo of the Mthethwa and built on military practices already developing in the region.

According to oral traditions and the accounts of the first European traders at his court, Henry Francis Fynn and Nathaniel Isaacs, Shaka reorganized warfare in several ways. He organized men by age into regiments that lived in military settlements and trained together. He favored a short, broad-bladed stabbing spear for close combat over throwing spears, used with a large cowhide shield. Tradition says he made his warriors go barefoot to move faster over rough ground.

The best-known reform is the battle formation called the buffalo horns. A strong central body, the chest, engaged the enemy head on. Two faster wings, the horns, ran out to surround the enemy's flanks and close behind it. A reserve, the loins, waited behind the chest, often seated with their backs to the fight so they would not get excited too early.

Within about a decade Shaka's warfare and conquests turned the Zulu into the dominant power in the region. The buffalo horns formation was still used by Zulu armies in 1879, when it overwhelmed the British camp at Isandlwana.
lesson: Lasting advantage comes from combining training, organization and tactics into one system. A small group can outgrow larger rivals by working differently, not just harder.
source: Henry Francis Fynn, The Diary of Henry Francis Fynn; Nathaniel Isaacs, Travels and Adventures in Eastern Africa (1836); Zulu oral traditions in the James Stuart Archive
caveat: Historians debate how many of these innovations Shaka actually originated, since the colonial sources tended to exaggerate his role.
